issues.description: Fast-path regex may skip unitless zero time values that the original code might flag
issues.detail: The regex /\dm?s/i requires a digit immediately followed by 's' or 'ms'. A declaration like `transition-delay: 0` (unitless zero, which CSS treats as 0s in time contexts) will not match and will be skipped entirely. If the original rule (via valueParser) detected unitless zero as a time value, this is a behavioral regression. In practice valueParser likely doesn't classify bare integers as time nodes, so this is probably safe — but worth verifying with a test for unitless zero in transition/animation timing positions.

issues.description: Regex pattern could be tightened to reduce false positives on the fast path
issues.detail: The pattern /\dm?s/i will match strings like 'comic1sans' or '1stop' that contain a digit followed by 's' but are not time values. These false positives are harmless (they fall through to the existing valueParser slow path) but do reduce the optimization's effectiveness on declarations with such substrings. A tighter pattern like /\d(?:ms|s)\b/i would be more selective. Not blocking — the current pattern errs on the side of correctness, which is the right tradeoff.

issues.description: No new test added to demonstrate the optimization preserves behavior
issues.detail: The changeset describes only a performance fix, and the diff contains no new test cases. Even a small unit test asserting that values like `1px`, `100%`, `0`, and `red` are no longer parsed (or simply that all existing tests pass) would document intent. Existing test suite presumably covers correctness, but a regression around unitless-zero or unusual unit strings would not necessarily be obvious without explicit coverage.

issues.description: Module-level regex name could be more descriptive
issues.detail: `HAS_TIME` reads well at the call site but the regex actually matches 'a digit immediately followed by s or ms' — a heuristic for likely-time, not a strict time matcher. A name like `LIKELY_HAS_TIME` or a brief comment explaining it is a fast-path heuristic (not authoritative) would prevent future maintainers from mistakenly treating it as a definitive check.

dissents.topic: Whether the regex's correctness vs. tightness tradeoff is right

positions.position: The current regex is intentionally loose — false positives just fall through to the slow path, false negatives would skip real violations. Loose-and-correct is the right call for an optimization. Ship as-is.
A tighter regex (with word boundaries and explicit ms|s alternation) would document intent more clearly and squeeze more wins out of the optimization. The cost is one extra character in the pattern.

CSS spec says unitless 0 is valid as a time. The fast-path regex skips it. Without seeing the original rule's behavior on unitless 0, we can't be sure this isn't a regression — a test should be added or behavior verified.

valueParser doesn't tag bare integers as time nodes, so the original rule was almost certainly already skipping unitless 0 in practice. This is a theoretical concern that the existing test suite would catch if it mattered.

review.summary: This is a small, well-scoped performance optimization: short-circuit declarations whose value contains no digit-followed-by-s/ms substring before invoking valueParser. The change is logically sound and unlikely to alter correctness in practice — the fast-path regex is intentionally loose, so any false positives simply fall through to the existing slow path. The main residual concern is whether unitless zero in time-accepting properties (e.g., `transition-delay: 0`) is handled identically to before; this is almost certainly fine given how valueParser tags nodes, but a confirming test would close the loop. No P0 or P1 blockers; recommend merging with optional polish (slightly tighter regex, a unit test pinning unitless-zero behavior, or a one-line comment that HAS_TIME is a heuristic fast-path).
